title: Genesis 32. The Cup of the Wrestling.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 32. The Cup of the Wrestling.
Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him.
When he saw them, Jacob said: This is God's camp.
He called the name of that place Mahanaim, Two Camps.
The angels that ascended and descended on the stairway at Bethel now appear on the road.
The dream has become a company.
The invisible traffic between heaven and earth is now visible.
Jacob names it, two camps.
God's camp and his.
The Cup that was carried out of Haran is now accompanied by the host that guards it.
Then Jacob sends messengers ahead to Esau his brother,
in the land of Seir, the field of Edom.
He commands them: Thus you shall say to my lord Esau:
Thus says your servant Jacob.
I have sojourned with Laban and stayed until now.
I have cattle, donkeys, flocks, male servants, and female servants.
I have sent to tell my lord that I may find favor in your sight.
Your servant Jacob.
The man who stole the blessing now calls himself the servant.
The man who took the birthright now sends gifts.
The man who fled from his brother's murder threat now approaches with humility.
The Cup that was stolen is now being returned,
not the blessing itself, but the posture.
Jacob bows before the one he wronged.
The messengers returned: We came to your brother Esau.
He is coming to meet you.
And four hundred men are with him.
Four hundred.
The last time Jacob saw Esau, Esau said in his heart:
Let the days of mourning for my father approach.
Then I will kill my brother Jacob.
Now Esau is coming with four hundred men.
The brother who was robbed is coming with an army.
Then Jacob was greatly afraid and was distressed.
The man who said if at Bethel,
if God will be with me, is now afraid.
The man who saw a stairway to heaven and heard God speak the covenant is now terrified of his brother.
The conditional faith that started on a stone pillow meets its first real test,
and it trembles.
He divided the people who were with him, along with the flocks,
the herds, and the camels, into two companies.
He said: If Esau comes to the one company and strikes it,
then the company which is left will escape.
The schemer schemes.
The man who divided his father's household by deception now divides his own household by fear.
If Esau destroys one camp, the other might survive.
The same calculation he made before deceiving Isaac,
what if I get caught, now applied to survival.
The Cup is held by a man who is preparing to lose half of it.
Then Jacob prayed.
God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, Lord,
who said to me: Return to your country and to your relatives,
and I will do you good.
I am not worthy of the least of all the steadfast love and all the faithfulness which You have shown Your servant.
For with only my staff I crossed this Jordan,
and now I have become two companies.
Deliver me, please, from the hand of my brother,
from the hand of Esau.
For I fear him, lest he come and strike me,
the mothers with the children.
But You said: I will surely do you good,
and will make your offspring as the sand of the sea,
which cannot be counted for multitude.
The first prayer Jacob prays in Scripture.
The man who said if, the man who set conditions on God,
now prays.
And the prayer begins with the same words he has been saying since Bethel:
the God of my father Abraham, the God of my father Isaac.
But then it shifts.
I am not worthy.
The man who grabbed a heel, stole a birthright, deceived a father,
schemed against an uncle, bargained for a wife, says:
I am not worthy.
The conditional if of Bethel has become the unworthiness of Jabbok.
The vessel that set terms now kneels.
He remembers: with only my staff I crossed this Jordan.
The man who left with nothing, a stone, a dream, a vow,
now stands with two wives, eleven sons, flocks, herds, servants, camels.
The Cup that was carried out empty is now full.
And the man holding it says: I did not fill this.
You did.
Then he quotes God back to God: You said,
I will surely do you good,
and will make your offspring as the sand of the sea.
The man who said if now says: You said.
The conditional has become a quotation.
The vow that started as a bargain has become a plea based on God's own word.
The vessel is still not clean.
But it is learning to argue from the right text.
He stayed there that night and took from what he had a present for Esau.
Two hundred female goats and twenty male goats.
Two hundred ewes and twenty rams.
Thirty nursing camels and their colts.
Forty cows and ten bulls.
Twenty female donkeys and ten foals.
He delivered them into the hands of his servants,
every herd by itself, and said: Pass over before me,
and put a space between herd and herd.
Five hundred and fifty animals.
The man who took a birthright for a bowl of stew now gives five hundred and fifty animals to the brother he wronged.
The grabber gives.
The taker returns.
Not the blessing, that cannot be returned.
But the wealth.
The fruit of twenty years of labor poured out as an offering to the one he robbed.
He commanded the foremost:
When Esau my brother meets you and asks you, saying,
Whose are you?
Where are you going?
Whose are these before you?
then you shall say: They are your servant Jacob's.
It is a present sent to my lord Esau.
Behold, he also is behind us.
He commanded the second, the third, and all who followed the herds:
This is how you shall speak to Esau when you find him.
You shall say: Not only that, but behold,
your servant Jacob is behind us.
Wave after wave.
Each herd arrives separately.
Each servant says the same thing: Jacob is behind us.
The brother who ran away is now approaching.
The brother who stole is now giving.
The brother who deceived is now coming in the open,
behind the gifts, but coming.
The Cup that was hidden in goatskin is now arriving with goats.
For he said:
I will appease him with the present that goes before me,
and afterward I will see his face.
Perhaps he will accept me.
Perhaps.
The man who said if now says perhaps.
The conditional faith has not disappeared.
But it has changed shape.
At Bethel, Jacob bargained with God.
Here, Jacob hopes for mercy from his brother.
The vessel is still uncertain.
But the uncertainty is now directed at reconciliation, not survival.
The present passed over before him,
and he stayed that night in the camp.
He rose up that night and took his two wives,
his two servants, and his eleven sons,
and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them and sent them over the stream and sent over what he had.
Everything crosses.
Two wives.
Two servants.
Eleven sons.
All the possessions.
All the household.
Everything that Jacob accumulated in twenty years crosses the river.
The Cup that was carried out of Haran is now carried across the Jabbok,
the river whose name means emptying.
The same root as, to wrestle, to embrace.
The river that empties is the river where God wrestles.
And Jacob was left alone.
The man who has been surrounded by people for twenty years, wives,
sons, servants, flocks, is now alone.
The man who schemed with people, bargained with people, deceived people,
served people, is now alone.
The Cup that was held by a household is now held by one man.
The vessel stands by itself at the river.
And a man wrestled with him until the breaking of dawn.
The text does not say who started it.
It does not say why.
A man, comes in the dark and wrestles.
Not a vision.
Not a dream.
A man.
The same word used when three men appeared to Abraham at the oaks of Mamre.
The same word used when the two angels came to Sodom.
A man.
At the river.
In the dark.
Wrestling.
The verb, is used only here in Scripture.
It is a word built from the dust,
the same dust God promised would number Jacob's offspring.
The man who was promised dust is now wrestling in the dust.
The Cup that was promised as dust is now being fought for in the dirt of a riverbank.
When the man saw that he did not prevail against Jacob,
he touched the hollow of his thigh,
and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was put out of joint as he wrestled.
A touch.
Not a blow.
Not a strike.
A touch.
The same word used when Isaac touched Jacob's goatskin hands.
But where Isaac's touch was deceived, this touch is truthful.
The man touches the hip,
the place where the covenant was sealed in circumcision.
The sign of the covenant is struck.
The flesh that was marked at eight days is now dislocated.
The Cup is cracked, not broken, not emptied, cracked.
The vessel that holds the promise is now marked with a wound.
But Jacob would not let go.
The man said: Let me go, for the day is breaking.
Jacob said: I will not let you go unless you bless me.
The grabber grabs.
But now he grabs God.
The man who took a heel, a birthright, a blessing,
now holds onto the One who gave the promise and refuses to release.
Not to steal.
Not to scheme.
To receive.
I will not let you go unless you bless me.
The first time Jacob has asked for a blessing instead of taking one.
The conditional if of Bethel has become the relentless grip of Jabbok.
The vessel that set terms now holds on without terms, except one:
bless me.
The man said: What is your name?
Jacob.
The question forces him to say his own name.
The name that means heel-catcher.
The name that means deceiver.
The name that has defined him since the womb,
the one who grabbed, who took, who supplanted.
Jacob says his name.
He confesses who he is.
The same question that was asked of Adam, where are you,
is now asked of Jacob: who are you?
And he answers with the truth.
The man said: Your name shall no longer be called Jacob,
but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men,
and have prevailed.
Israel.
The name changes.
Not because Jacob became worthy.
Not because he stopped being a deceiver.
Because he wrestled.
Because he held on.
Because when the hip was struck,
and the body was wounded and the day was breaking,
and the man said let me go, Jacob said no.
The grabber became the wrestler.
The man who took from people is now the man who refuses to let go of God.
The name Israel contains the word, to strive, to persist, to contend.
And, God.
He strives with God.
Not against, with.
The wrestling is not rebellion.
It is the most intimate form of persistence.
The man who could not wait for God to fulfill the oracle now clings to God until God fulfills it.
The conditional if has become a grip that will not release.
Jacob asked: Please tell me your name.
The man said: Why is it that you ask my name?
And he blessed him there.
The same response God gave to Moses when Moses asked His name at the burning bush,
but in reverse.
There God said: I AM.
Here the man says: Why do you ask?
The name is not given.
The blessing is given.
The Cup is not explained.
It is poured.
The vessel does not receive a label.
It receives a wound and a new name and a blessing it did not earn.
Jacob called the name of the place Peniel,
For I have seen God face to face,
and yet my life has been delivered.
Peniel.
The face of God.
The man who deceived his father's face,
who covered his own face with goatskin, has now seen God's face.
The man who hid behind a tent flap and behind a veil and behind a lie has now stood face to face with the One who sees.
And he survived.
The Cup that was carried through every deception and every arrangement and every scheme is now held by a man who has seen God and lived.
The sun rose on him as he passed over Penuel,
and he limped because of his thigh.
The sun rose.
The same word used when the sun set at Bethel.
The sun that set when Jacob arrived with nothing now rises when Jacob leaves with a wound and a name.
The man who slept on a stone and dreamed of a stairway now limps across a river with a dislocated hip and a new identity.
The dreamer has become the wrestler.
The grabber has become the one who clings.
He limps as the sun rises.
The children of Israel do not eat the sinew of the hip to this day,
because Jacob was touched there in the wrestling.
Genesis witnesses the limp as he leaves the encounter and the remembered mark in Israel's food custom;
it does not tell us how long Jacob's limp lasted.
The vessel that holds the Cup is marked,
not by what it did, but by what it received.
The Cup is cracked.
The name is changed.
The sun has risen.
Jacob, now Israel, limps toward the brother he wronged.
The man who sent gifts ahead and divided his camp and calculated his losses now walks with a limp.
The schemer has met someone he cannot outmaneuver.
Jacob names the place Peniel because he says he has seen God face to face,
but Genesis leaves the wrestler's identity unresolved in the narration.
The Cup of the covenant, given, cut, sealed, tested, inherited, stolen, dreamed,
labored, bargained, returned,
is now held by a man who will never walk the same again.
The name is new.
The body is marked.
The vessel is cracked.
And through the crack, through the wound, through the limp,
through the name that was changed in the dark, the Cup pours.
Not because the vessel is clean.
Because the vessel held on.
